nameStory: The name 'black-eyed Susan' comes from the flower's striking appearance - bright yellow petals radiating around a dark brown or black center, like a cheerful face with a big dark eye. The 'Susan' part likely comes from an old English ballad about Sweet Black-Eyed Susan, making this wildflower sound as friendly and approachable as it looks.
description: Black-eyed Susan is a cheerful wildflower that looks like a golden daisy with a dark chocolate center. These sturdy plants grow up to 3 feet tall and produce bright yellow flowers with distinctive dark brown centers that really do look like eyes. The whole plant has a rough, fuzzy texture and blooms abundantly through summer and fall, making it one of New England's most recognizable wildflowers.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like flowers with 10-20 petals surrounding a prominent dark brown or black dome-shaped center that feels firm and bumpy to the touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Rough, hairy leaves that feel like coarse sandpaper; lower leaves are spoon-shaped while upper leaves are narrower and clasp the stem

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright plants 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems, often growing in patches or colonies

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant feels distinctly rough and bristly due to stiff hairs covering stems and leaves - you'll notice the scratchy texture immediately

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Dark center develops into a cone packed with small black seeds that rattle when shaken in late fall

habitat: Black-eyed Susan thrives in sunny, open areas throughout New England including fields, meadows, roadsides, and prairie-like spaces. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun, often appearing in disturbed areas, abandoned lots, and along woodland edges. You'll commonly find it growing alongside goldenrod, Queen Anne's lace, and other sun-loving wildflowers.

seasonality.spring: New fuzzy rosettes of rough, sandpaper-like leaves emerge from the ground, growing into small clumps before sending up flower stalks.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant bright yellow flowers opening from June through August, attracting bees, butterflies, and other pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Flowers continue blooming into September and October while seed heads develop into dark, cone-shaped structures full of seeds that birds love.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to the ground, but the dark seed heads often persist on dried stalks, providing winter food for goldfinches and other seed-eating birds.

funFact: Black-eyed Susan flowers aren't actually single flowers at all - each 'flower' is made up of dozens of tiny individual flowers packed together, with the yellow 'petals' being ray flowers and the dark center containing up to 500 tiny disc flowers, each capable of producing its own seed!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other yellow daisy-like flowers, but black-eyed Susan's distinctive dark brown center and rough, sandpaper-textured leaves set it apart. Remember: if it feels scratchy and has a chocolate-dark center, it's your black-eyed Susan!
contextualKnowledge: Black-eyed Susan is Maryland's state flower and was traditionally used by Native Americans for medicinal purposes, though the plant is actually toxic to cats and should be kept away from feline friends. Despite being a native wildflower, it's also popular in gardens and has many cultivated varieties.
compareHints: Among its Rudbeckia relatives, black-eyed Susan is distinguished by its rough, hairy texture and moderate size. Brown-eyed Susan has smaller flowers and deeply lobed leaves, while cutleaf coneflower grows much taller with deeply divided, almost fern-like leaves. Orange coneflower has similar flowers but smoother leaves and a more orange-yellow color.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Rudbeckia family, cutleaf coneflower is the giant with the fancy haircut - it's much taller than black-eyed Susan and has those distinctive deeply-divided leaves that no other coneflower possesses.
Among the Rudbeckia family, brown-eyed Susan stands out for its smaller flowers and brown (not black) centers.
Orange coneflower differs from black-eyed Susan by forming spreading colonies rather than individual clumps, and has slightly more orange-tinted petals.
Among its Rudbeckia relatives, sweet black-eyed Susan stands out for its impressive height and fragrant flowers.

Great coneflower's towering 8-foot height immediately distinguishes it from all other Rudbeckia species in New England - black-eyed Susan tops out around 3 feet, cutleaf coneflower reaches about 4-6 feet, and orange coneflower stays under 3 feet.
Unlike its Rudbeckia cousins, clasping coneflower has small chaffy scales (like tiny bracts) beneath its ray petals that other black-eyed Susans lack.
